entries.topic: The word 'Hebrew': ʿIvri in the Bible, its disputed etymology, and the Hebrew language from vernacular to revival

claims.text: Genesis 14:13 calls Abram 'Abram the Hebrew' (Hebrew ha-ʿIvri); it is the first use of the word ʿivri in the Bible.

The rabbis of Genesis Rabbah (41) already gave several explanations of the word: that Abram stood on one side and the whole world on the other; that he descended from Eber (Genesis 10–11); or that he came from across the river (the Euphrates). Friedberg calls the term 'slippery'.

The origin of ʿIvri is uncertain. Britannica says it may come from ʿever, 'the other side', perhaps for Abraham's crossing from beyond the Euphrates or the Jordan; the link to the ancestor Eber is the other traditional reading. Neither is settled.

In the Hebrew Bible, 'Hebrew' is mostly a name that other peoples use for the Israelites, or that Israelites use about themselves when speaking to foreigners (for example Potiphar's wife, Pharaoh, and the Philistines in 1 Samuel); it is rarely their ordinary self-designation.

Britannica gives a conventional sequence of names: 'Hebrews' for the patriarchs' descendants up to the conquest of Canaan, 'Israelites' from then until the Babylonian exile, and 'Jews' after the return from exile. This is a reference-book convention, not a rule the ancient texts follow consistently.

Many scholars have connected ʿIvri with the Ḥabiru/ʿApiru, a socially marginal class named in second-millennium BCE Near Eastern texts. There is no consensus: Naʾaman, for example, holds that the two groups had nothing in common apart from a similar social status.
Britannica says the name 'might' be related to the Habiru known from Egyptian inscriptions of the 13th–12th centuries BCE, which signals a possibility, not an established identification.
Hebrew is a Semitic language. Britannica places it in the Northwest Semitic branch, alongside Aramaic and the other Canaanite languages.

Scholars date the end of Hebrew as an everyday spoken language differently. The usual range is c. 200–400 CE. Mishnaic Hebrew (c. 1–200 CE) was still spoken, and it began to fall out of daily use within about a century of the Mishnah (c. 200 CE). Some reference works place its death as a native language in the 4th century, and the Academy of the Hebrew Language says that from the 5th century CE it was no longer anyone's everyday spoken language.

Britannica dates the start of the decline much earlier: it says Western Aramaic began to supplant Hebrew from about the 3rd century BCE. Spoken Hebrew therefore declined gradually over several centuries, and no single cut-off date applies.
Aramaic became the main spoken language of Jews in the region. The Jerusalem Talmud (c. 350–400) and the Babylonian Gemara (c. 500) discuss the Hebrew Mishnah mostly in Aramaic.

Hebrew did not survive 'only in prayer and scripture'. It remained in wide literary use until the modern revival: liturgical and secular poetry (piyyut, Shmuel HaNagid, Judah HaLevi), some legal contracts, philosophy and science (through Hebrew translations of Arabic works), and grammar and lexicography (Saʿadya Gaon, Judah ben Ḥayyuj). The Academy also notes that some Jewish travellers and schools went on speaking it.

Eliezer Ben-Yehuda (born Eliezer Perelman, 1858, in Luzhky, Lithuania; died 1922) moved to Jerusalem in 1881 and raised Ben-Zion Ben-Yehuda, described as the first modern Hebrew-speaking child. He began publishing his dictionary in 1910; the full 17-volume Complete Dictionary of Ancient and Modern Hebrew was finished only after his death.

Ben-Yehuda did not revive Hebrew alone. Teachers who adopted Hebrew as the language of instruction in schools played a large part, and the Language Council he co-founded was later succeeded by the Academy of the Hebrew Language.
Britannica says Hebrew was revived as a spoken language in the 19th and 20th centuries and is the official language of Israel.
The Knesset passed Basic Law: Israel – The Nation State of the Jewish People on 19 July 2018, by 62 votes to 55 with two abstentions.

Section 4 of that law states that 'the state's language is Hebrew', gives Arabic a 'special status' (its use in state institutions to be regulated by law), and says the section does not harm the status Arabic held in practice before the law.

NPR, reporting on the law, said it removed Arabic's earlier status as an official language and replaced it with the 'special status'. Arab members of the Knesset condemned the law; the government said it codified long-standing features of the state.

entries.topic: Who is Jewish: halakhic, movement and legal definitions; secular Jews; diversity; world population

claims.text: Being Jewish is understood both as belonging to a people and as belonging to a religion. Pew notes that some Jews see Jewishness mainly as religion, while others see it as culture, ancestry, or a combination of these.
Under traditional Jewish law (halakha), a Jew is anyone born to a Jewish mother or converted to Judaism in a halakhic manner.
Israel's Law of Return (section 4B, added in 1970) uses a similar definition: a person born of a Jewish mother, or who has converted to Judaism, and who is not a member of another religion.

On 15 March 1983 the Central Conference of American Rabbis (Reform) resolved that the child of one Jewish parent, mother or father, is under a 'presumption of Jewish descent', to be confirmed by 'appropriate and timely public and formal acts of identification' such as a Hebrew name, Torah study or Bar/Bat Mitzvah.

Movements do not recognise one another's definitions uniformly. Israel's Chief Rabbinate, which controls Jewish marriage in Israel and applies traditional halakha, does not treat everyone admitted under the Law of Return as Jewish for marriage.
Pew's 2020 survey estimated about 7.5 million Jews in the United States (5.8 million adults and 1.8 million children), or about 2.4% of US adults.

Pew found that 27% of US Jewish adults are 'Jews of no religion': people who describe themselves religiously as atheist, agnostic or 'nothing in particular' but who consider themselves Jewish in other ways, such as ancestry or culture.
In Pew's 2020 survey, 92% of US Jewish adults identified as non-Hispanic White and 8% as Hispanic, Black, Asian, other or multiracial; among Jews aged 18–29 the share was 15%.

The Jews of Color Initiative's 'Counting Inconsistencies' meta-analysis, carried out by Stanford researchers in 2019, estimates that 'at least 12–15%' of American Jews are Jews of colour and argues that earlier population studies undercounted them. Its definition and method differ from Pew's, so the two figures are not directly comparable.

In 1973 Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi Ovadia Yosef ruled that the Beta Israel of Ethiopia were Jews and called for them to be brought to Israel. Operation Solomon in 1991 airlifted over 14,000 Ethiopian Jews to Israel.
Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics counted 168,800 residents of Ethiopian origin at the end of 2022: about 92,100 born in Ethiopia and 76,800 born in Israel to Ethiopian-born fathers.
JNS reported that CBS figures released before Sigd in November 2025 put Israel's Ethiopian Jewish population at 177,600 in 2024. The CBS release itself was not fetched.

India had three main historic Jewish communities. The Bene Israel trace their origin to a shipwreck of seven Jewish families at Navagaon near Alibag, south of Mumbai, and numbered about 20,000 in 1948. The Cochin (Malabar) Jews of Kerala spoke Judeo-Malayalam and hold copper plates bearing a charter traditionally dated to about 1000 CE. The Baghdadi Jews came in the British era, to Calcutta from 1798 and to Bombay with David Sassoon in 1832.
Most Indian Jews have emigrated, chiefly to Israel; the Jewish Virtual Library puts India's present Jewish population at about 4,500.
Most historians date a Jewish community in Kaifeng, China, to the Song dynasty (960–1279); a stele of 1489 records a synagogue in 1163. Yu (2017) disputes this and argues for arrival under the Yuan.

Estimates of people with Kaifeng Jewish ancestry today are about 600–1,000 (a 2008 estimate), of whom perhaps 40–50 take part in Jewish activities. China does not list them among its 55 recognised minorities. Because they lack proof of descent under Israeli and Orthodox criteria, the few who have moved to Israel (about 19, with help from Shavei Israel) underwent formal conversion.

The Jewish Agency, using data from demographer Sergio DellaPergola of the Hebrew University, put the world's Jewish population at 15.8 million at the start of 2024, including about 7.3 million in Israel and 6.3 million in the United States. Its count is based on self-identification as Jewish and/or having at least one Jewish parent, without belonging to another religion.
Israel's CBS, in its Rosh Hashanah release of 9 September 2026, put the world Jewish population at nearly 15.9 million as of 1 January 2026, about 46% of them in Israel (as reported by i24NEWS).
The CBS Independence Day 2026 release states that at the end of 2024 about 45% of the world's Jews lived in Israel, and that about 81% of Israel's Jews were born in Israel.

entries.topic: Israeli: citizenship vs registered 'nationality'; who the CBS counts; population by group (2026)

claims.text: 'Israeli' properly means a citizen of the State of Israel, whatever the person's religion or ethnicity. The CBS population count is wider: it includes Israeli citizens and 'permanent residents without Israeli citizenship' listed in the Population Register.

In its Rosh Hashanah release of 9 September 2026 (preliminary figures), the CBS put Israel's population at about 10.305 million: about 7.828 million 'Jews and others' (78.3%), about 2.173 million Arabs (21.7%), and about 304,000 foreign nationals.

The 78.3% and 21.7% shares add up to 100% without the foreign nationals. They are therefore shares of the roughly 10.0 million Israeli residents, not of the 10.305 million total; as shares of the total they are about 76% and 21%.

The same release reported growth of about 124,000 (1.2%) over the year: about 182,000 births, about 50,000 deaths, about 24,000 new immigrants, and about 57,000 Israelis leaving the country against about 21,000 returning.

The CBS Independence Day release of 19 April 2026 gave 10.244 million: 7.790 million Jews and others (76%), 2.157 million Arabs (21.1%) and 296,000 foreign nationals (2.9%, an end-2025 figure). Israel had 806,000 people in 1948 and has received over 3.5 million immigrants since.

CBS defines 'Others' as non-Arab Christians, members of other religions, and people not classified by religion in the Population Register. Most are immigrants who came under the Law of Return or through family reunification and are not registered as Jews.
CBS's 'Arabs' category comprises Muslims (including Circassians), Arab Christians (including Armenians) and Druze.

Recent CBS headline releases combine Jews with 'others'. The most recent separate count of Jews found in this session is 7,208,000 in 2023, about 73% of the population, as cited by Wikipedia from CBS.
By religion, CBS data put Israel's Muslim population at about 1.849 million at the end of 2025 (18.6% of residents).

CBS estimated about 184,200 Christians in Israel in December 2025 (about 1.9% of the population). At the end of 2024, 78.7% of Christians were Arabs, and Arab Christians made up 6.8% of the Arab population.
CBS counted about 150,000 Druze at the end of 2022 (preliminary): 1.6% of Israel's population and 7.4% of its Arab population. About 81% lived in the Northern District and 19% in the Haifa District.

CBS population figures have included the residents of East Jerusalem since 1967 and the Druze and Muslim population of the Golan since 1982. Israeli localities in the West Bank (Judea and Samaria) are also included.

Most Palestinian residents of East Jerusalem hold Israeli permanent residency, not citizenship. In 2020 the Times of Israel reported that about 20,000 had acquired citizenship, out of roughly 350,000.
Wire reports on CBS figures note that they include Palestinian residents of East Jerusalem, whose 1967 capture and later annexation by Israel are not recognised internationally.

Most Golan Druze long held permanent residency rather than citizenship. About 20% had naturalised by mid-2022, and by March 2026 roughly 40% across the four Golan Druze towns had taken Israeli citizenship.

Israel's Population Registry records 'nationality' (le'om) separately from citizenship. The courts treat the le'om entry as statistical data with no probative weight, whereas citizenship is registered with evidential value.

In CA 8573/08 Ornan v. Ministry of the Interior (2 October 2013), the Supreme Court (President Grunis, Justices Melcer and Vogelman) rejected a petition to register 'Israeli' as a nationality. It held that the appellants had not shown, by objective criteria, that a distinct Israeli nationality exists, and it followed the 1972 Tamarin precedent (CA 630/70).
The Law of Return, passed on 5 July 1950, states: 'Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh.'

The 1970 amendment (Amendment No. 2, 10 March 1970) extended these rights to the child and grandchild of a Jew, to the spouse of a Jew, and to the spouses of a Jew's child and grandchild, but not to a person who was a Jew and voluntarily changed religion. It also added the definition of 'Jew' in section 4B. As a result, some immigrants are eligible to enter without being registered as Jewish.

entries.topic: Zionist: origin of the word, forerunners, Herzl and Basel, varieties, Jewish opposition, Christian Zionism, polling

claims.text: Zionism is a political movement and ideology that aimed at, and since 1948 has supported, a Jewish national home and later a state in the Land of Israel/Palestine. The Basel Program of 1897 is its founding statement.

Nathan Birnbaum coined 'Zionist' and 'Zionism' in 1890, in his periodical Selbst-Emancipation, and 'Political Zionism' in 1892. He later left the movement, became an advocate of Diaspora cultural autonomy and Yiddish, and in 1919 became the first Secretary General of the Orthodox Agudath Yisrael.

Proto-Zionist forerunner: Rabbi Judah Alkalai (1798–1878), Sephardi rabbi of Zemun near Belgrade, wrote Minḥat Yehuda (1843). After the 1840 Damascus affair he called for an 'Assembly of Jewish Notables' to organise settlement in the Land of Israel, funded by a tithe, and he settled there himself in 1874.

Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Kalischer's Derishat Ẓiyyon (Lyck, 1862) argued that the redemption promised by the prophets would come by natural means, 'by self-help', and proposed buying and farming land in Palestine, with an agricultural school and a Jewish guard.

Moses Hess (1812–1875), a socialist, published Rome and Jerusalem in 1862. It argued that Jews would remain a 'homeless people' until they had their own country; ignored at first, it later influenced Ahad Ha'am and Herzl.

Leon (Leo) Pinsker, an Odessa physician, turned from assimilationism after the 1881 pogroms. He published Auto-Emanzipation anonymously in 1882, became a leader of Ḥibbat Ẓiyyon (Ḥovevei Ẓiyyon, 'Lovers of Zion'), and convened the Kattowitz Conference in 1884.

The First Aliyah (1882–1903) began with 14 Bilu members who landed at Jaffa on 6 July 1882. Nearly 35,000 Jews came in this period, mostly from Eastern Europe with some from Yemen, and almost half left within a few years. Settlers founded moshavot such as Rishon LeZion, Rosh Pina and Zichron Ya'akov.

Baron Edmond de Rothschild began supporting the colonies in late 1882. He sent Rishon LeZion an agronomist and 30,000 francs in November 1882 and took Zmarin (later Zichron Ya'akov) under his patronage. The Jewish Virtual Library says his aid kept the early settlements from collapse.

Theodor Herzl's Der Judenstaat ('The Jews' State') was published on 14 February 1896 in Leipzig and Vienna. It discussed both Argentina and Palestine as possible territories and insisted on legal sanction from the ruling power rather than gradual 'infiltration'.

The First Zionist Congress met in the Stadtcasino, Basel, on 29–31 August 1897, with about 200 participants from 17 countries (69 of them delegates of Zionist societies). It founded the Zionist Organization and elected Herzl president.

The Basel Program, adopted on the Congress's second day, opens: 'Zionism aims at establishing for the Jewish people a publicly and legally assured home in Palestine' (other translations: 'secured under public law'). It lists four means: settlement of farmers, artisans and traders; organisation of Jews; strengthening of Jewish national feeling; and steps toward obtaining government consent.

Zionism took several forms. Political Zionism (Herzl, Nordau) sought a legally recognised home through diplomacy. Practical Zionism (Lilienblum, Pinsker) put immediate settlement first. Synthetic Zionism (Weizmann) combined the two. Labour Zionism (Syrkin, Borochov, Ben-Gurion) joined socialism to settlement.

Further currents: Religious Zionism (Reines, who founded Mizrachi; Rav Kook) saw building the state as a religious duty. Revisionist Zionism (Jabotinsky, who founded the Revisionist party in 1925) sought sovereignty on both banks of the Jordan and argued for an 'iron wall'. Cultural Zionism (Ahad Ha'am) sought a spiritual and cultural centre rather than mass migration or statehood.

In 1903 the British Colonial Secretary Joseph Chamberlain agreed in principle to Jewish settlement in East Africa (the 'Uganda' scheme; the land lay in present-day Kenya). The Sixth Zionist Congress voted 295–178 in August 1903 to send an investigative commission, and the Seventh Congress rejected the plan in 1905. Israel Zangwill's Jewish Territorial Organization then pursued other territories.

Jewish opposition (Reform): the Pittsburgh Platform of American Reform rabbis (16–19 November 1885) declared, 'We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community', and rejected a return to Palestine. Reform revised this position in the 1937 Columbus Platform.

Jewish opposition (socialist): the General Jewish Labour Bund, founded in Vilna on 7 October 1897, was anti-Zionist from its start. It promoted doikayt ('hereness'), meaning Jewish life and Yiddish culture where Jews already lived, and national-cultural autonomy.

Jewish opposition (Haredi): Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum of Satmar argued in Vayoel Moshe (1961), drawing on the Talmud's 'Three Oaths', that Zionism is incompatible with Judaism. Neturei Karta, founded in Jerusalem in 1938 by Amram Blau and Aharon Katzenelbogen after breaking with Agudath Israel, rejects the State of Israel; it numbers in the low thousands, and Satmar and other Haredi bodies have publicly disavowed its activities.
Present-day Jewish anti-Zionism: Jewish Voice for Peace, a national US organisation since 2005, declared in January 2019 that it is 'unequivocally opposed' to Zionism.

Non-Jewish Zionism: Christian Zionism, rooted in 17th-century English Puritan 'restorationism' and later in John Nelson Darby's dispensationalism, supports Jewish return to the Holy Land on theological grounds. Not all Christian Zionists are dispensationalists, and several Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant bodies reject the ideology.

The Blackstone Memorial of 1891, organised by the Christian restorationist William Blackstone, petitioned President Benjamin Harrison to 'give Palestine back' to the Jews. Sources give the number of signatories differently, 431 or 413.

Christians United for Israel was incorporated by Pastor John Hagee in February 2006. CUFI announced in December 2020 that it had passed 10 million members; this is CUFI's own figure, and it has published no definition of 'member' or method of counting.

Polls of US Jews on calling themselves 'Zionist' diverge sharply. A JFNA survey (fielded March 2025, reported February 2026) found 37% Zionist, 8% non-Zionist, 7% anti-Zionist and 48% none of these. A JPPI opt-in panel (June 2024, 634 respondents) found about 80% 'Zionist' or 'slightly Zionist'. A Milwaukee federation study (2024–25) found 43%. Federation leaders attribute part of the gap to disagreement over what the word means.
In Pew's 2020 survey, 58% of US Jewish adults said they were at least somewhat emotionally attached to Israel. Pew did not ask about the 'Zionist' label.
